Hi everyone. For my project, I looked at whether economic news helps explain why consumers feel worse than headline economic indicators might suggest. My main finding is that news tone helps a simple economic model, but that benefit weakens once I include broader conditions and previous sentiment. I also found that the sources emphasize different economic issues, which affects what the news measure actually represents. I will focus on those findings and what I think we can reasonably conclude from them.

For the text analysis, I used 670 economic titles from NPR, Colorado Sun, and Hacker News. I coded whether each title described adverse, mixed, or favorable economic conditions, using automated labels. I also measured topic words and price framing, and checked selected numerical claims against official releases. To build the monthly index, I averaged the labels within each source and then weighted the three sources equally. This gave me 47 balanced months. After aligning the dates with the economic data, I had 45 usable observations and 21 months for evaluating predictions.

One issue I checked was whether the classification approach worked consistently on different titles. The hybrid classifier agreed with the automated reference labels on 68 percent of titles in development evaluation. On a separate set of 300 titles, agreement fell to 53.3 percent. The two reference sets differ, but the drop still warns against assuming that development performance will carry over. I therefore kept the failed classifier comparison visible and used the saved automated coding for the primary index. Those labels remain provisional, so I interpret the results cautiously.

The source comparison shows why the choice of text matters. Housing words appear in about 31 percent of the Colorado Sun sample, compared with 10 percent of Hacker News titles. Inflation-rate wording shows the reverse pattern: about 20 percent for Hacker News and 3 percent for Colorado Sun. My interpretation is that a tone index partly reflects which problems a source covers. A source discussing housing pressure can sound negative while accurately reporting household difficulties. Equal weighting helps with differences in volume, but these three sources still cannot represent the whole media environment.
News helps only the narrower model

I then tested whether the monthly tone index improved sentiment predictions. All four bars use the same 21 evaluation months. The measure is RMSE, so lower is better. Adding tone to the simple economic model reduces error from 12.07 to 10.82. But that improvement is uncertain because its confidence interval includes zero. The more useful comparison is the lower pair. Broader controls without tone give an error of 5.82. Adding tone gives 6.06. So the larger improvement is already there without news. That is why I cannot credit the overall improvement to media tone.
Last month already tells us a great deal

I also compared the models with a simple alternative: predicting that sentiment stays at last month's level. That gives an error of 4.09. Broader controls plus previous sentiment give 3.98, while adding tone increases error to 4.32. This tells me that recent sentiment already contains a lot of useful information. My original tone measure does not show a dependable extra forecasting benefit once that information is included. This is a finding about this measure and sample, rather than evidence that news never matters.
Different wording can describe the same fact

The factual examples helped me separate tone from bias. For the July 2020 GDP release, a 32.9 percent annualized decline corresponds to roughly a 9.5 percent decline over the actual quarter. Both numbers can describe the same event, although they sound quite different without the units. So a negative or alarming headline is not automatically inaccurate. The context matters. These examples show why I would avoid interpreting a negative tone score as a direct measure of bias. They also do not tell us how readers actually responded.

My conclusion is that the simple economic model misses important information, but our original news-tone measure does not reliably improve the broader forecast comparisons. A dictionary measure does better in one secondary check, so I keep that result as a reason for further investigation. In practice, I would use the index to monitor the economic conversation and investigate unusual sentiment gaps. I would want stronger evidence before relying on it for forecasting. The sample is small, the labels are provisional, and the economic data include revisions. To test causality, the next step would be an experiment comparing equally truthful framings of the same information. Thank you.
